I want to learn more about this topic of computer science. I love to know how the internals of my programming language works. I've done some courses on language design and finite state machines, where should I take my learning from here?
What are the best resources for leaning about programming language and compiler theory?
hackershelf.com has a ton of e-books about programming. Maybe you can find something useful there.
this is an amazing resource, thank you so much
Your next stop should be digital electronics. This is where you get to the real deal. Start with Arduino, from there you can go to Arm and FPGA's.

I have an Arduino and have been playing around with it, but I'm more interested in how finite grammars are transformed into programming languages and how they are transformed into instructions capable of being understood by a computer

Which is why you need to know how the actual silicone does what it does. For example how does an 8bit adder work? As soon as you figure that out you can figure out what a compiler needs to do to make that happen.
I see, that makes a lot of sense, actually

I would recommend the edX online course Circuits and Electronics presented by Agrawal and Sussman, both chip designers. Beware that it is deemed as "weed them out" type of course by many engineers, so not exactly easy. But it should be possible to follow trough the digital gate design which is all you need at this stage.

Also check out the wiki pages of those guys. They have written books on most of what you are trying to learn.

Hi Voaters, Welcome to /v/Ecommerce - Please take the time to introduce yourself.

I'm a UK based digital marketeer with a background in software development and project management. I manage a small team of international marketeers, covering 12 markets in 4 languages, across two brands.

My passions are the latest in PPC innovations and SEO strategies.

I'm a geek of all things data. I work as an ecommerce business analyst for a UK based brand in a strong growth phase (+30-50% PA for the last 5).

Really what interests me is how a small brand and a small team can capitalise on the opportunities provided by the latest technology and services to gain a competitive advantage over larger brands who are not able to be agile in the marketplace. I'm obsessed with ROI and driving down costs, so I end up playing accountant with new project appraisals. So I'm always on the lookout for new opportunities that can (genuinely) give us an edge which is really how the business I work for thrives.
Hi Crashing. Out of interest, are you selling a product or a service?

We sell our own branded product B2C, we are able to offer a really strong value proposition for the fact that we can have the same spec or better product as our competitors but with a selling price half of what our competitors are at. We are essentially an Aldi of our market segment. However because we manage the whole supply chain from product design and sourcing to fulfilment to the customer we are able to retain good margin even at a lower selling price.

The big challenge in being 'an Aldi' type is that you are always fighting uphill against recognized brands and it's very easy if you're not careful to go overboard on the media spend chasing sales targets, which is why we have to be extremely discerning in which opportunities to pursue and promote. It's both annoying and amusing though when you see how clunky some of the competitors eCommerce operations are - but it doesn't really matter if they're not optimising like mad because their brand carries them.
